## Proof

**Yes**, the distribution of $y^{(1)}$ first-order stochastically dominates that of $y^{(2)}$.

**Setup.** Let $Z = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} a_i x_i$ denote the common part. Since $x_1, \dots, x_{N-1}$ are independent of $x_N$, the random variable $Z$ is independent of $x_N$ in both settings. We may write
$$y^{(1)} = Z + a_N x_N^{(1)}, \qquad y^{(2)} = Z + a_N x_N^{(2)},$$
where $x_N^{(j)} \sim h^{(j)}$ and $Z$ is independent of each $x_N^{(j)}$.

**Step 1: FOSD is preserved under non-decreasing maps.** The hypothesis $H^{(1)}(t) \le H^{(2)}(t)$ for all $t$ means $x_N^{(1)} \succeq_{\text{FOSD}} x_N^{(2)}$, i.e., $P(x_N^{(1)} \le t) \le P(x_N^{(2)} \le t)$ for all $t$. Since $a_N \ge 0$, the map $g(t) = a_N t$ is non-decreasing. For any $s$,
$$P(a_N x_N^{(1)} \le s) = P(x_N^{(1)} \le s/a_N) \le P(x_N^{(2)} \le s/a_N) = P(a_N x_N^{(2)} \le s)$$
(with the inequality direction preserved because $a_N \ge 0$; the case $a_N = 0$ is trivial since both sides equal $Z$). Hence
$$a_N x_N^{(1)} \succeq_{\text{FOSD}} a_N x_N^{(2)}.$$

**Step 2: FOSD is preserved under convolution with an independent variable.** Let $W^{(1)} = a_N x_N^{(1)}$ and $W^{(2)} = a_N x_N^{(2)}$, so $W^{(1)} \succeq_{\text{FOSD}} W^{(2)}$, and $Z$ is independent of both. For any threshold $t$,
$$P(y^{(1)} \le t) = P(Z + W^{(1)} \le t) = \mathbb{E}\big[\,P(W^{(1)} \le t - Z \mid Z)\,\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[\,F_{W^{(1)}}(t - Z)\,\big],$$
and similarly $P(y^{(2)} \le t) = \mathbb{E}[\,F_{W^{(2)}}(t - Z)\,]$. Since $F_{W^{(1)}}(s) \le F_{W^{(2)}}(s)$ for every $s$ (by Step 1), taking expectations over the same random variable $Z$ preserves the inequality:
$$P(y^{(1)} \le t) \le P(y^{(2)} \le t) \quad \text{for all } t.$$

**Conclusion.** This is precisely the definition of first-order stochastic dominance: $F_{y^{(1)}}(t) \le F_{y^{(2)}}(t)$ for all $t$. Therefore the distribution of $y^{(1)}$ first-order stochastically dominates that of $y^{(2)}$. The two key ingredients are (i) $a_N \ge 0$, ensuring the scaling map is non-decreasing so FOSD of $x_N$ is preserved, and (ii) independence of the common sum $Z$ from $x_N$, ensuring FOSD is preserved under addition of the shared term.
